subsection: 5. Eggs: structure, nutritional significance and contribution to the diet

points: Shell: porous calcium carbonate that protects the contents and allows gases to pass through.
Shell membranes: two thin membranes lining the shell that help keep out bacteria.
Air cell: a pocket at the blunt end between the membranes, which enlarges as the egg ages and indicates its freshness.
Diagram: cross-section of an egg, labelling shell, shell membranes and air cell.

notes.b: The two liquid parts of the egg are held in place by structures that anchor the yolk at the centre.
points: Albumen (white): surrounds the yolk and is a watery mixture of proteins, mainly albumin, ovalbumin and globulin.
Chalazae: two cord-like strands of albumen that anchor the yolk in the centre of the egg.
Yolk: a rich, yellow centre surrounded by the vitelline membrane, containing fat, lecithin, cholesterol, proteins, vitamins and minerals.
Germinal disc: a small spot on the surface of the yolk, which would develop into a chick if fertilised.
Diagram: the albumen, chalazae, vitelline membrane, yolk and germinal disc, labelled on the same cross-section.
Protein is about 13% of the egg and is high biological value (HBV), with a biological value of 100%.
White protein: albumin, ovalbumin and globulin. Yolk protein: vitellin and livetin.
Fat is about 12%, almost all in the yolk, and is mostly saturated and finely emulsified by lecithin.
The white is fat-free; cholesterol is found only in the yolk.
Eggs contain no carbohydrate and no fibre.
Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are found in the yolk.
B group vitamins are found in both the white and the yolk, including B1, B2, niacin and B12.
Eggs lack vitamin C.
Minerals make up about 1% of the egg: calcium, phosphorus, zinc and sulphur, with iron in the yolk.
The egg is about 75% water.
Free-range eggs can contain higher levels of some vitamins, such as niacin and B12, than eggs from caged hens.

notes.h: Contribution of eggs to the diet
points: Eggs are cheap, nutritious and suitable for people on low budgets.
Eggs are a protein alternative to meat and fish.
Eggs supply HBV protein for lacto-vegetarians, who eat dairy products and eggs.
Eggs are easily digested, so they suit children, older people and convalescents.
Eggs are quick and easy to cook, and are versatile in sweet and savoury dishes.
Eggs can be eaten alone, or with toast or other carbohydrate foods to make a meal.
Eggs contain saturated fat and cholesterol, so intake should be moderate for people limiting cholesterol.
Eggs should be served with complex carbohydrate, fibre and vitamin C foods to balance the diet.

keyTerms.definition: The white of the egg, a watery mixture of proteins that surrounds the yolk.
The yellow centre of the egg, rich in fat, lecithin, cholesterol, vitamins and minerals.
Two cord-like strands of albumen that anchor the yolk in the centre of the egg.
The pocket at the blunt end of the egg between the shell membranes, which enlarges as the egg ages.
One of the two thin membranes lining the shell, which help keep bacteria out.
The small spot on the yolk surface, which would develop into a chick if fertilised.
The main protein in the egg white, which is high biological value.
A person who eats dairy products and eggs but no meat or fish.

questions.prompt: Name three parts of an egg and give the function of each.
questions.model: Shell: protects the contents and allows gases to pass through. Albumen: supplies HBV protein and cushions the yolk. Yolk: supplies fat, fat-soluble vitamins, iron and lecithin. Chalazae: anchor the yolk in the centre. Air cell: indicates the freshness of the egg, enlarging as it ages. Any three parts with functions give full marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the nutritive value of eggs and explain how eggs contribute to the diet of different groups of people.
questions.model: Nutritive value: about 13% HBV protein with 100% biological value (albumin, ovalbumin and globulin in the white; vitellin and livetin in the yolk); about 12% fat, mostly saturated in the yolk, with lecithin and cholesterol; the white is fat-free; no carbohydrate or fibre; fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K in the yolk; B group vitamins in both parts; minerals including calcium, phosphorus, iron and zinc; no vitamin C; about 75% water. Contribution: HBV protein for growth and repair in children and adolescents; easily digested for older people and convalescents; protein for lacto-vegetarians; cheap, quick and versatile for families on low budgets; should be served with carbohydrate and vitamin C foods, and eaten in moderation by people limiting cholesterol.
